To really examine the situation in Canada and the situation in the provinces as that member from the New Democratic Party did, and refer to the financial experts who analyse this continuously, we should refer to the last report of the Economic Council of Canada which examined the debt positions, borrowing positions, and spending positions of all provinces, specifically four, as it dealt with regional disparity and high unemployment in those particular provinces. The council suggested that some of the burden be lifted from the shoulders of the federal government and placed on the shoulders of the provincial governments to alleviate high unemployment. They also suggested that they use their own fiscal manoeuvrabilities. But in that report the Economic Council of Canada offered the final resolution that each provincial government-except the Newfoundland government-could use its own fiscal manoeuvrability.
To understand why they said that and why it is so important, we must go back to the previous studies, in which they showed that to service the debt alone was a massive problem. They showed, for instance, that the direct and indirect debt less the sinking fund, as a proportion of the personal income of Newfoundlanders, was too high. It was very high. We must then come to the conclusion that, in a situation like that, there is no fiscal manoeuvrability whatsoever-or very little, if any. That is something that must be considered when discussing this bill to borrow $7 billion.
The most important thing to be considered, however, is how that money is spent-what is done with it. In other words, priorities must be established. If we are to believe the Minister of Finance in his recent public statements, then we accept that the government must spend money to increase productivity in Canada-that must be their most important objective.
Politically speaking, I suppose it is a good thing for the Minister of Finance to go down to his own riding of St. John's West, as he did last week, and open a $55 million arterial road that he was partially responsible for getting. I suppose it is politically advantageous for him to turn around next week and open up a $44 million water system for which he negotiated when minister of intergovernmental affairs in the provincial government. It will do his soul good in another couple of months to announce as step one for an outer ring road in the same city a $35 million expenditure. That is fine, Mr. Speaker, politically speaking.
Apart from the fact that there are a lot of municipalities in Newfoundland who believe the old farmer's adage that money is like manure, of very little use unless it be spread, there is the question of the wise use of money and that of productivity. It is not nice at this time of year to see on the northeast coast of Newfoundland incredible dumping of fish every day because it cannot be sold and markets cannot be found. It is bad enough to know that when that Fish is sold, 80 per cent of it goes to the

October 25, 1979
Borrowing Authority
United States and other countries to be processed into a finished product. That is bad enough, but when you have an action, the first one taken by this government, to cut out and freeze boat building subsidies, and to cut out wharf construction affecting the primary producer, that is worse. It is interesting that the Minister of Finance is able to rationalize those decisions when he asks for $7 billion to be okayed by this House for his borrowing purpose.
It should also be very interesting to find out how the Minister of Finance will rationalize the recent cuts of his bosom pal, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) who decided to cut out filling job vancancies, to cut out term employees from being rehired, to cut out capital expenditures for construction in Newfoundland, which were all across-the-board decisions. I do not know how one can rationalize that when one looks at the figures and realizes that the federal government has spent less per capita on wages and salaries for federal employees in Newfoundland, that is, less per capita than any other province in Canada, and yet the across-the-board cut was taken.
It is interesting that just one week ago the President of the Treasury Board in answer to a question posed by one of my colleagues from Quebec said he was going to re-examine a departmental cut in light of the economic conditions in that hon. member's riding. The President of the Treasury Board said he had an open mind, and he repeated that statement. I thought, as many other members from high unemployment areas thought, that the President of the Treasury Board would then go to work and cancel all cuts in every high unemployment area in Canada, especially in Newfoundland. He had an open mind, he said. Yet, two days after that, he reiterated his policy of continued cuts, non-hiring for job vacancies, and continued the freeze on construction jobs.
It is obvious that the President of the Treasury Board has an open mind, in fact so open as to be totally vacant. It is important for the Minister of Finance to rationalize those decisions that affect those high unemployment areas of Canada, and especially in Newfoundland, when he asks for permission to borrow $7 billion. It would also be interesting for the Minister of Finance and for the government to remember that the people of Canada now believe that as government politicians it is a very good example of those who shake your hand before the election, and shake you after the election.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT 1979-80 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY FOR 1979-80
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in partaking of this debate, I would like to read some items into the record. In many ways I think the bill placed before us by the government is a contradiction of the statement that inflation is enemy number one. We are being asked to provide the government with some $7 billion in borrowing, and yet one of the major causes of inflation is the imbalance that we have in our service charge, being the interest that we have to pay out. This is probably one of the major reasons why the Canadian dollar has fallen in value, and in turn is the major reason why we see the rise in inflation. In fact, going through my notes I notice that Mr. Rob Douglas, when he was director of the now defunct centre for the study of inflation and productivity, said

that an analysis of the impact of the dollar's devaluation on domestic inflation shows that about one-third of the inflation was caused by the dollar's drop.
There is an insanity which seems to be at work here. In order to solve that insanity we just create more insanity. In order to wrestle with inflation, we take the steps which create even more inflation. It is an insane situation, and one I do not think members of this House should support. Obviously members of the government knew they should not be supporting measures of this kind when they were in opposition, but now they seem to go along with the pattern that was established by the former government.
I do not understand why they are caught in this type of rigid reality. I do not understand why they have not been able to introduce some new thinking, or bring some new imagination or put new light on the problems, including economic problems, which this country faces.
For the record I would like to read part of an article written in the Financial Post. Normally I am not a great fan of the Financial Post, but in the October 20, 1979, edition an article appeared posing some interesting questions. The writer suggested that members of Parliament should be asking these questions of the governor of the Bank of Canada and of the government as a whole. The questions read as follows:
1.	Bouey stressed the need to reduce inflation when announcing the latest bank rate increases. But would he have raised interest rates (as he has done three times since the Tories came to power) if the U.S. had not first raised its rate?
2.	Assuming, for now that Canada must generally follow the upward sweep in U.S. interest rates, does Bouey agree with the recent hikes by the U.S. Federal Reserve Board?
3.	What's needed, and how long would it take, to give Canada an independent monetary policy?
4.	How can a credit crunch that especially hurts small business cut inflation? Indeed, how, precisely, will high interest rates make the North American rate of inflation come down? Hardly anyone would quarrel with the idea that money-supply growth is closely related to inflation over, say, five years. But doesn't the high U.S. inflation rate (consumer prices up 11.8 per cent in August from a year ago) have more to do with oil prices and higher food costs than a money supply that's out of control?
5.	How long and deep a recession will it take to cool out inflation? Will wage demands really be any lower even at 8 per cent, 9 per cent or 10 per cent unemployment?
6.	To move inflation down to, for example 6 per cent from 9 per cent, someone has to take less of an increase in profits and wages. Who will this be: Small companies? Large companies? Unionized employees? Other workers? Farmers? Everyone equally?
7.	Even though the bank rate was increased seven times, from 7'A per cent to 11 VS per cent, between March, 1978 and January, 1979, short-term interest rates in Canada for a time fell below rates in the U.S. and the Eurodollar market. Allowing for the various factors that influence the flow of money, does the Bank have any evidence that the lower short-term rates during this period directly prompted a shift of money away from Canada?
They are good questions, and I hope the minister will be able to supply answers. It is the net outflow of capital that is pretty well the major source of the economic problems that we have. In 1975 the balance came in at a $4.75 billion deficit, up 225 per cent from the year before. In 1976 it dropped to $3.8 billion, in 1977 increased to $4.1 billion, and last year was a
October 25, 1979

record $5.2 billion. These deficits have created heavy pressures on the exchange rate, and the Canadian dollar has thus become worth less.
As I pointed out before, the devaluation of the Canadian dollar has become a major reason why we are in an inflation type of spiral. The devaluation of the dollar, the increase in food costs and the increase in oil costs are the major reasons why we are facing inflation, not some monetary policy that the governor of the Bank of Canada was trying to explain to us earlier in the day.
Since Canada is a major importer of food, some $3 billion last year, the loss of value of the Canadian dollar increased food costs. In 1978 the food price index was 216. It hurts the whole economy, increases unemployment and welfare rates and strikes at the viability of many small businesses. For example, in Saskatchewan some 51,000 new jobs were created from January to August, a pretty good rate for Saskatchewan. The premier is quoted as saying most of those increases occurred in the small business sector.
What will higher interest rates proposed by this government do to the small businessman? Banking acquaintances in Regina tell me there has been a general slowdown in business in my constituency because of the increase in interest rates. There is a general fear and sense of insecurity. There is no sense of certainty. There is no ability to predict and plan. How high will interest rates go; 15 today, 16 tomorrow, 17 next week, 18, 19, 20? Is there no end in sight?
The people of this country want some assurance, some predictability, and some leadership. We keep floundering along following the same impotent policies introduced by the former government. This government in its own madness is continuing those. All at once we see members of the former government being relieved of this insanity, and in fact demanding that this insanity be stopped. Why is it this only occurs on the opposition side and never on the government side? It would be better for the people of this country if the government were able to snap itself out of the foolish reality in which it is caught.
Major economic problems result in the over-all balance of payments deficits which cause devaluation and in turn exacerbate other problems such as large price increases. This continues to increase the problem and feeds itself. What caused the imbalance in the first place? We are made to understand the service trade is the major problem, some $5.2 billion last year. What is the origin of that? The origin of that, unfortunately, is the economic history of this country, the type of development that both the Liberal and Conservative governments sponsored.
We have had quick development for the sake of quick development. We sold our resources. We allowed foreign capital to come in and develop our resources. They took the resources out and left us with a debt. Now the chickens have come home to roost. Now we have to pay off the debt.
Let us look at the scope of foreign ownership in this country. StatsCan reported in 1976 that of the 230,262 non-financial
Borrowing Authority
enterprises in Canada, 3,630 or 1.5 per cent were classified as foreign owned. In terms of statistics, 1.5 per cent is not a very large number, yet the 1.5 per cent, the small handful of foreign-controlled corporations, had 34.9 per cent of all Canadian sales, 31 per cent of the total assets, and 46 per cent of the profits generated in this country in 1976. That blows my mind.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT 1979-80 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY FOR 1979-80
speechtext: That wouldn't take much.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT 1979-80 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY FOR 1979-80
speechtext:
The hon. member says that would not take much. Does it not blow his mind that 1.5 per cent of all non-financial Canadian companies that are foreign-controlled take nearly half of all profits in this country? Is that not disturbing? Is it not obvious why we have the type of economic problems that we do in this country? All that profit is sent outside our borders. It is the return on past investments, and that is the price we now have to pay. That is why we have a deficit in our balance of payments, a devalued Canadian dollar, and spiralling inflation.
What is the solution? More borrowing, more indebtedness to foreign banks, more interest rates to be paid? It is the insanity that keeps repeating itself, insanity upon insanity upon insanity. Do we need a crash to wake the government up and make it realize that we are set on a course that will result in a great amount of human suffering? Small businessmen, farmers, working people and old people trying to exist on meagre incomes, living on the edge of economic survival, will be swept under by the forces the government opposite is setting loose.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT 1979-80 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY FOR 1979-80
speechtext: What about Saskatchewan?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT 1979-80 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY FOR 1979-80
speechtext:
The hon. member mentioned Saskatchewan. I did want to close with that. Saskatchewan, a small province of less than a million people, under an NDP government has taken an initiative in tackling this basic economic problem. They have tried to control resources developed in Saskatchewan so that the benefits of those resources stay in the province and stay in this country. That is why the people of Saskatchewan own nearly 50 per cent of the potash. Members opposite might claim that this is communism, and put that government down.
I am reminded of the day when the present Secretary of State (Mr. MacDonald) was in my home city of Regina. When asked what he thought of the takeover of potash by the provincial government, he said the only criticism he had of it was that it took so long. Mr. Speaker, he knew the solution to Saskatchewan's economic problems. But where is his voice now? Where are the voices of those Conservatives who know better? We heard them when they were in opposition. Are they to be stilled?
What sort of force is it in cabinet and in government which makes the voice of reason, understanding and enlightenment silent in a moment of need? Is there some hidden force which obliges people to do things they know do not make any sense at all?

October 25, 1979
Borrowing Authority
In Saskatchewan we are involved in potash and in the development of our resources such as oil. The people have a stake in this development so that when profits accrue they stay in the country and they help with the balance of payments rather than become an irritant and create a problem. The members who sit in this little corner have the solution to the Canadian economic problem, and that is Canadian ownership in which the public and government play an active part. Until we are willing to tackle the basic problem of foreign control we shall go on and on, I suppose, until a crash occurs. Is that what it takes before we learn? I hope not, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, addressing myself to this bill I want to make it clear at the outset that my approach to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) is somewhat different from that of some of the speakers on my left.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT 1979-80 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY FOR 1979-80
speechtext: I hope so.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT 1979-80 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY FOR 1979-80
speechtext:
I want to deliver a message of encouragement, of optimism, of hope, even of charity. I have a well-known company in my city-it's head office is in my riding- and I propose to borrow, if I may, a term they use. They have a motto "Steinberg's is on your side". I should like the Minister of Finance to know that many of us are very much on his side as he accepts the difficult challenges which face the country, as well as the many opportunities which lie ahead for Canada in this his first year as minister.
Benjamin Franklin once said that those who gave up an essential liberty to purchase a little temporary safety deserved neither liberty nor safety. That statement is very appropriate for politicians in the late seventies and eighties here in Canada. I say this because we have to make difficult decisions.
In some areas the Minister of Finance has made difficult decisions. In others, though, he has not done so. Fie has, if you like, traded essential liberty, which I would define in certain circumstances as being equated with a sound economy, for temporary safety which in some respects is equivalent to political credibility.
The minister was faced with making a decision on a very difficult problem, that of the mortgage interest deductibility scheme advocated by his party during the election. It is our impression that it was only with great reluctance that the minister put forward even his modified version of that scheme, but that scheme is an example of what I mean, of giving up something which is in the interests of all Canadians, in the interest of a sound economy, in order to purchase a certain amount of political credibility. That is a black mark on the minister's record.
In addition, the hon. gentleman is supporting the position of the government in other economic areas, such as its stand on oil prices. It is an article of faith on the part of hon. members opposite, this thesis of letting oil prices rise to world market levels. I am myself a great believer in the marketplace; indeed,
I am very supportive of the principle of free enterprise. But in the case of oil we are dealing with an international cartel. We

are not dealing with a normal market situation; we are dealing with circumstances which are probably unique in recent history. This being the case, the concept of looking always to the market place is completely out of place in the current economic scheme. It is pushing us into inflation, pushing us inevitably into difficult times. The governor of the bank, according to the statement he delivered, expects an increase in oil prices and contemplates a rate of inflation considerably more than we are presently seeing.
Then there is question of the government's attitude to PetroCan. This is another policy which the minister indicates he supports as an article of faith. I find it difficult to believe that members opposite uniformly support the principle of privatization as an article of faith. As a matter of fact I recall the maiden speech of the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko) when he talked about the experiences he had had with Crown corporations. It is small wonder, because we know that the government of Alberta which carries the Tory colours probably has as many Crown corporations as any other government in the country, if not more. So I find it hard to believe that privatization per se should be regarded as an article of faith.
But, again I do support the concept of privatization. Private ownership of the means of production is an article of faith with me. But there are certain areas today in which the private sector cannot be expected to meet the challenges which face society. In an earlier speech I made here I drew an analogy between PetroCan and other kinds of ventures into which governments are necessarily being drawn. Take, for example, space exploration in the United States. Should that be the concern of the private sector? Does anyone seriously suggest that individual investors could invest in a project of that kind from which the rewards, even if they were tangible, could easily be delayed for a hundred years? That is not the kind of investment which private investors in this day and age are prepared to make. I suggest in the case of the energy sector in this country, and for that matter in many countries, that we are dealing with a similar situation.
As a government hon. members opposite have an obligation to make certain kinds of investments which are investments for society as a whole. That is what we are dealing with in the case of Petro-Canada, and I hope that eventually hon. members opposite will abandon some of these articles of faith and look at the reality of Canada and the necessity of having a strong Canadian public company in the energy sector.
We have heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) himself identify our public enemy number one as inflation. Who could disagree? Inflation sets class against class and groups against groups. Everybody is trying to maintain or perhaps increase their share of the national income. Inflation indeed is a social malady, as Carl Beigie recently wrote. It is a terrifying prospect. Panic all of a sudden has beset our own community and other nations, and it must be addressed and arrested. Tough decisions are going to be required to bring that about.
October 25, 1979

I might say that beginning in 1975 the previous government started making many tough decisions. One of the tough decisions was to establish a monetary stance of some kind and to establish targets for monetary growth, and that policy was consistently followed. Another tough decision was to reverse trends which had been established with regard to the expansion and growth of the public service. Those decisions were carried out, but those trends continued, and they were in play and effective on "black Monday", May 22.
Then another area in which the government acted was that of reducing the rate of government spending. This was also a tough decision, finally culminating, on an accelerated basis, in what is sometimes referred to as the August exercise of 1978. That was not a popular decision. It was difficult, and no minister and no government can expect to be popular when faced with that kind of choice. There are always serious trade-offs for those kinds of decisions. The Minister of Finance will be expected to continue in that tradition as he carries out his responsibilities. That is what we are looking to him for. That is what all Canadians are looking to him for.
We are not looking for cop-outs like the mortgage tax credit scheme, and I say that as a member who at one time supported an idea of limited mortgage interest deductibility. But with study came enlightenment, and I know the minister has suffered through the same pangs of realizing that he is faced with a scheme which is not only neutral in its application but also detrimental, particularly in the current economic climate in this country where we are faced with inflation. What kind of scheme do we have? We have one that is likely to put even more upward pressure on mortgage interest rates, and one which all observers conclude is definitely going to put pressure on housing costs and increase housing costs. So the minister did not make a tough decision. He was not prepared to take political credibility on the chin with regard to that decision.
On the other hand, 1 have to be fair in my judgments, and 1 must also say that nobody wants high interest rates. I deplore high interest rates. We have heard the NDP deploring high interest rates. The minister has made the decision to impose high interest rates. I am sure he made that decision with the best of good will and intention. This problem must have been studied. We have Governor Bouey. We have the Minister of Finance. The decision was a tough one. I am not prepared to say at this point that it was the right decision, but I admire the minister for having the guts to step up and say, "We have to make some tough decisions, and this is one of them".
Within the context of the statement by Benjamin Franklin which I cited earlier, the minister has not backed down, but he needs help. He needs help from everybody. He needs help from us, and I hope we are going to be able to play a creative and positive role in helping him to develop the policies which are required to meet the number one problem of inflation.
We see what the minister is doing on the monetary side. We see increases in interest rates. We are not satisfied. At least I am not satisfied that that in itself is going to solve the problem. It seems to me that monetary policy may be somewhat deficient in that we continue to have great liquidity and
Borrowing Authority
do not seem to be curbing credit, but nevertheless he has established his monetary stance and monetary position.
What about the fiscal side? We can look forward to the minister's budget, and we look forward to it with great anticipation, but unfortunately he is on a bad wicket with his mortgage tax credit, and let us hope that the cost of that program, which is estimated to be in excess of $2 billion when it is in effect, will not pre-empt and compromise other programs which the minister inevitably must introduce if he is going to come to grips with the problems which face this country.
I have a number of suggestions for the minister-none of which he will probably accept-and they are not to be introduced immediately in any event, but I do think that the minister has to offer us programs destined to stimulate the supply side of our economy and get more capital-Canadian capital, preferably-into plant and equipment and into research and development. We do not need any greater stimulation of aggregate demand at this time, as this mortgage tax scheme is likely to create. What we need are sound fiscal programs designed to attract Canadian savings into productive sectors of our economy, not into the real estate sector, not into MURBs at this point, but into those areas where we can expect to improve efficiency, produce goods, and supply services at reduced cost. I certainly do not think I am alone in putting that forward as a sound proposal in terms of one approach at the fiscal level to deal with this incredibly difficult problem of inflation.
We hear a lot of rubbish, sometimes amusing rubbish, from our friends on the left. We hear a lot of criticism. Our friends on the left try to put hon. members opposite and ourselves all in the same category, which I do not accept. 1 think there are very major policy differences. Nonetheless, I cannot let this opportunity pass without making reference to some of the extraordinary arguments and propositions I hear coming from my friend, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Rae), who was elected to this House at the same time I was. There is no doubt but that he should know better. 1 see he has disappeared from the House.

subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-PRORATA PENSIONS FOR CERTAIN WIDOWS-INTRODUCTION OF AMENDING LEGISLATION
VETERANS AFFAIRS-PRORATA PENSIONS FOR CERTAIN WIDOWS-INTRODUCTION OF AMENDING LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. McKinnon) for being here tonight to comment on my question which I asked on Wednesday, October 17, as reported at pages 298 and 299 of Hansard.
Before I get into the question, and certainly before we get any further into this session, perhaps the minister would be happy to join with me in paying tribute to the work which was done in this field by his predecessor, the Hon. Daniel J. MacDonald.

subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-PRORATA PENSIONS FOR CERTAIN WIDOWS-INTRODUCTION OF AMENDING LEGISLATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-PRORATA PENSIONS FOR CERTAIN WIDOWS-INTRODUCTION OF AMENDING LEGISLATION
speechtext:
We all know of the difficulty he had getting money for veterans out of the cabinet of the last few years, but he fought hard and won quite a few gains for our veterans. We all know that there were a number of things that Mr. MacDonald hoped he might yet win, and that leads me to say that I hope his successor will finish the job he tried to do.
On October 17 my question was in two main parts. Principally 1 asked about amendments to the Pension Act which would make it possible for widows of veterans to receive the widow's pension where the veteran's disability pension was below 48 per cent. This is a cutoff which has been most unfair through all the years and for all the decades it has been there. Time and again there have been recommendations by outside committees and by standing committees on veterans affairs that this be changed, at least to the extent of having a prorata pension for widows where the veteran's disability pension was below 48 per cent. My hunch and my feeling is that we are getting closer to it. I hope the minister might be able to give us that assurance tonight. I realize he cannot give us the details until he presents his bill, but if he can assure us that the bill will be coming in soon, that would be deeply appreciated.
[Mr. Johnston.)
When 1 questioned the government House leader today about future business, I said that I hoped something like this could be announced and put before us this year before November 11.
When the minister responds, I hope he will also say anything he can about other measures which ought to be considered. One is to put the basic rate of the disability pension on a basis which ties it to the average income of the five designated categories in the public service. As the minister knows, we tied it to that level some years ago, but provided only for its indexing according to the rise in the cost of living. The result has been that year by year the amount of the 100 per cent disability pension gets behind the composite rate which was accepted as fair. We adjusted it once. Why not put it on a fixed basis so that it will always keep pace with that composite level?
Also there is the question of certain improvements which still need to be made to the compensation for former prisoners of war. I am sure these have been drawn to the attention of the minister. I hope that some time during this session something might be done in that area.
The other very large area where something needs to be done is in revising the War Veterans Allowance Act. This is an old piece of legislation which was brought in back in the 1930s when on the civilian side we had an old age pension with a means test. The war veterans allowance matched that and did something a little better for veterans than what was done for civilians. Times have changed. The old age pension situation is a little better. We got rid of the means test, at least for the basic amount. But some of those old trappings are still there with respect to the war veterans allowance. It seems to me the time has come, especially in view of the other social changes and in view of the years since two or three wars were fought, for the war veterans allowance to be turned into a guaranteed annual income for veterans at a certain age below the age at which ordinary people go on pension.
There are a number of issues of that kind about which I am concerned, and I am hoping that in this session, with the minister's keen interest in veterans, and despite the fact he has got two jobs, he will be pushing hard for the kinds of improvements to which I have been referring tonight. There are others, but I believe I have named the main ones, namely, altering that 48 per cent rule so that widows where the husband's rated disability was below 48 per cent will get a pension as of right; doing something about fixing the 100 per cent basic disability pension so it will stay with the composite level that was agreed upon; improving the compensation for former prisoners of war; and bringing the War Veterans Allowance Act up to date so that it will meet the needs of our veterans today.
1 am happy to welcome the hon. member for Victoria to this important post of veterans affairs, and I look forward to working with him and with other members who are interested in veterans affairs so that we can make some real progress during this session on behalf of Canada's veterans, their families and their survivors.
October 25, 1979

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-REVIEW OF PERSONNEL MANAGEMENT AND THE MERIT PRINCIPLE-APPLICATION OF PRINCIPLES IN REPORT
PUBLIC SERVICE-REVIEW OF PERSONNEL MANAGEMENT AND THE MERIT PRINCIPLE-APPLICATION OF PRINCIPLES IN REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week I rose in the House to ask the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) about the curious new rulings which have been made by the deputy commissioner of corrections regarding the disposition of so-called surplus employees at the B.C. penitentiary. I put the question to him that he has added an additional principle to the D'Avignon report in which he now invokes a "reverse order merit" principle. 1 suggest somewhat facetiously, but not entirely facetiously, that if we applied that principle to the administrators of the penitentiary service in the Pacific region, the quality of work would go up dramatically.
I say that because I wonder if the regional director of the penitentiary service in British Columbia has any other qualifications beside the fact that his brother is the senior officer in the Solicitor General's department here in Ottawa. His sidekick, Babalouie, or whatever his name is, worked with him in Kingston. The inspector general who was sent out to do an audit on the work methods and the number of employees there, was as effective as sending lettuce by rabbit. I wonder if the man who is in charge of the penitentiary has any other personal interests except the fact he is a retired man from the military and feels that this is a good way of supplementing his military pension. One does not get a very sanguine picture of the administration in the Pacific regional district.
Specifically, 1 have been dealing with the case of a constituent of mine who has ten years of service at the penitentiary and who held a senior position in his classification. This man was acting supervisor of that area for two years. He has taken the management course offered to him by the penitentiary service. He also received a letter from the acting director general of the Public Service Commission saying, "we hope that you will soon be getting a promotion".
However, when the previous government instituted a firing policy of 5,000 employees, the B.C. penitentiary service decided to do an audit and to check on these employees and, lo and behold, this man who has ten years service is the first to go, or at least almost the first to go. I wonder why? An evaluation was done on him, but when he asked to see that report, he was refused. He appealed it and his appeal at the regional district was turned down, whereupon he appealed to the commissioner here in Ottawa. This is what the commissioner had to say with regard to the force reduction committees. They:-
-assess the qualifications of persons so identified and rate them in accordance with the reverse order of merit principle.
He says rates them, he does not say dismisses them. Something is rotten in the state of Denmark when there is that kind of evaluating going on in the public service. My question to the

October 25, 1979
Adjournment Debate
President of the Treasury Board was to the effect: how long can we have a public service when we have that kind of assessment being done on the public servants? What kind of sense of security will there be in the public service when that kind of chopping is going on? Everyone will be wondering who will be next.
Perhaps one of the liabilities of this gentleman was that he was one of the 16 hostages at the time of the Mary Steinhaus-er affair at the penitentiary. Perhaps he knows too much of what is going on inside the penitentiary. It may be that one of his liabilities is that he had the audacity to protest some of the decisions made at the penitentiary regarding staff and the lack of promotions to officers.
It seems to me that any administration that tries three times to hire a person and put him in an acting supervisory position when that person does not have the qualifications is hardly the kind to qualify for judging this person, who has all the necessary qualifications on paper, who has the experience necessary, and who has done the things asked of him. But he is released. As I say, something is wrong in the state of Denmark.
Two things are wrong with the disposition of this case, according to the act. First, he was not allowed to see his assessment. It was secret; he never saw it. When he complained, they made another one. Finally, he appealed to the deputy commissioner. The act says that he is supposed to receive a response from the deputy commissioner in 30 days but, Mr. Speaker, it took 95 days for that response to get back to this individual.
I suggest that if the D'Avignon report is dealing with the merit principle-and I say this in all seriousness and not at all facetiously-the regional director, his deputy, the man who is in charge of the penitentiary, ought to be subjected to that principle of reverse order of merit that they are now invoking with respect to this employee. In that way the system in the specific regional district would be cleaned up in a hurry.
I have sent notices to the Solicitor General (Mr. Lawrence) regarding some of the activities which are occurring in the hiring practices, and some of the inequities that the employees feel are carried on. It is time that we invoke the merit principle in order of merit and keep those people who have seniority, who have proficiency, and who have shown consistency in their work patterns-keep them, and deal with the administrators who are perpetrating this act of injustice on the employees.

speakeroldname: Mr. Scott Fennell (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-REVIEW OF PERSONNEL MANAGEMENT AND THE MERIT PRINCIPLE-APPLICATION OF PRINCIPLES IN REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's question touches on an issue which is of great importance to us, that of the application of the merit principle in the hiring and dismissal of public servants. I should like to review briefly where we stand at the moment.
The Public Service Employment Act, in respect of lay-offs, states that where the services of an employee are no longer required because of lack of work or because of the discontinu-

ance of the function, the deputy head, in accordance with regulations of the commission, may lay off the employee. The specific regulation concerned is section 33.IB of the public service employment regulations. Where two or more employees are employed in similar positions and one must be laid off, the deputy head must lay off the employees in order of merit. The order of lay-off begins with the employee lowest on the list. This is known as the "reverse order of merit" and should ensure that the best employees are the last to be laid off.
The government recognizes the subjectivity involved in this process, and would be pleased to draw to the personal attention of the Chairman of the Public Service Commission any cases such as that referred to by the hon. member where it is felt that the process may not have been implemented fairly. The minister will meet to review the situation with the chairman in the near future. I would encourage all members to write the minister with details of these cases as soon as possible. The government does not accept that abuse has necessarily occurred, but believes the matter to be of such importance to the fair practice doctrine which underlies government employment that detailed scrutiny of its operations by members of the commission is clearly justified.
As we all know, the D'Avignon report on the review of personnel management and the merit principle was tabled in this House recently. This will provide an opportunity to hon. members and the government to themselves consider the broad application of the merit principle within the federal public service, with a view to safeguarding its continued and even expanded application throughout the federal departments and agencies of the Crown.

subtopic: FISHERIES-COD QUOTAS IN GULF OF ST. LAWRENCE
FISHERIES-COD QUOTAS IN GULF OF ST. LAWRENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 17 I put questions to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. McGrath) about supplementary cod quotas in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and the matter of allowing boats 100 feet and over to fish in those water. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans in the previous government prohibited boats over 100 feet from fishing in Gulf waters to preserve the stocks for Gulf-based coastal and deep sea fishermen. That measure allowed New Brunswick and Quebec fishermen to increase their catches in the past two years. As an example, Mr. Speaker, Quebec catches increased 30 per cent a year in the past two years.
The minister said there were consultations with the Atlantic provinces and Quebec at a meeting held in St. John's, Newfoundland, in mid-July. According to my information, supplementary cod quotas in the Gulf of St. Lawrence for the years 1979 and 1980 were discussed but the committee never agreed to let trawlers 100 feet and over in the gulf. The representatives of the province of Quebec suggested at that meeting of the Atlantic Groundfish Advisory Committee a supplement of
10,000	metric tons of cod. No province expressed objections to the increased quotas.

October 25, 1979
The minister was informed by the advisory committee on July 11 that a supplement for boats over 100 feet could be challenged by certain provinces and, of course, coastal fishermen. Here, Mr. Speaker, is an excerpt from the minutes of that committee, and 1 quote:
Cod stocks in area 4T seem in better shape. Members are generally in favour of an increase in the current TAC (total authorized catch); however, the possibility of a TAC increase and allocations to boats over and under 100 feet bring out contradictory opinions-
A few days later, the minister received a working paper entitled "The Minister's Briefing Notes," in which the civil servants bring up the same problems. I quote:

If the quota is increased by this amount in 1979, the inshore fleet segment will be happy. However, knowing that the scientific advice suggests we can increase by as much as 13,000, the offshore segment will be most vocal in their objections. Conversely, allowing the large vessels to catch up to this amount of fish in 4T (an area currently excluded to vessels greater than 100 feet) would be totally unacceptable to the inshore fishermen,... and such a policy would be violently opposed by the provinces of Quebec, New Brunswick, and P.E.I.
Mr. Speaker, the inshore fishermen are against increased quotas for vessels greater than 100 feet, and rightly so. For them, and those who work in the processing plants, their families, the towns where they live, access to those resources is indispensable.
In his press release of August 27 advising the fishermen of higher quotas, the minister took them by surprise, and especially the governments of Quebec, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, by authorizing vessels of more than 100 feet, which belong to big companies, to catch 6,000 additional tons in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and that, to the detriment of inshore fishermen.
Mr. Speaker, a few days after making his decision on August 27, the minister stated at a conference on northern cod, and 1 quote:
Our policy, my policy on this matter is simple and well-defined. Coastal fishermen have priority access to this resource.
You will certainly agree, Mr. Speaker, that this minister wears many hats.
Like several other members, Mr. Speaker, I am wondering whether the hon. minister has one policy for the coastal fishermen of Newfoundland, another for those of New Brunswick, another for those of Quebec, and finally another favouring large companies. Indeed, why did he authorize vessels greater than 100 feet to catch 6,000 metric tons of cod in the Gulf when no, I repeat, no favourable recommendation to this effect was made by the Atlantic Groundfish Advisory Committee or in the working paper that he received from his officials?
Adjournment Debate
Mr. Speaker, the government has often boasted that it could come to an agreement with the provinces on any subject. I can therefore not understand how the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans can decide to let trawlers of 100 feet or more into the Gulf of St.Lawrence knowing that the provinces of Quebec, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, as well as the coastal fishermen of the Gulf, including those of Newfoundland, have expressed disagreement about his new policy. Mr. Speaker, the minister has unilaterally made a decision which is unacceptable to eastern Canada.
Since this new policy will have unfavourable effects on the fishing industry of Quebec, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland, as well as Cape Breton Island, I ask on behalf of my colleagues from eastern Quebec and eastern Canada that the hon. minister postpone his decision until the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry has studied the matter.

speakeroldname: Mr. Thomas Siddon (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subtopic: FISHERIES-COD QUOTAS IN GULF OF ST. LAWRENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for Gaspe for outlining these problems.

I am pleased to comment on the issue raised by the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Cyr) and, in so doing, to establish the facts and events as they happened. The management of all the Atlantic groundfish fishery is based on recommendations made by the Atlantic Groundfish Advisory Committee. The provinces, the industry, and the fishermen's associations are all represented on that committee.
At the July 11, 1979, meeting of AG AC, the possibility of increasing the 1979 total allowable catch for the southern Gulf was discussed. Scientific advice indicated that there was room to increase the total allowable catch by some 13,000 tons over the 36,000 already allocated for that fishery. Following that meeting, further consultation with representatives of vessels under 100 feet indicated that they required 4,000 tons to carry their fishery to the end of the fishing season. This means in effect that 9,000 tons were left to be allocated, and representatives of vessels over 100 feet were quite anxious to have all that quota. However, in order not to affect the 1980 total allowable catch and to be on the safe side, the Minister of Fisheries decided to authorize the allocation of only 6,000 tons to the larger vessels. These vessels will not commence fishing until after November 1.
I think it would have been irresponsible for the minister not to allocate at least part of the recommended increase, when the scientific advice suggested this could be done in accordance with sound conservation principles. The hon. member would probably have criticized the minister if he decided not to allocate that quota. In allocating Gulf stocks, the minister has made it clear that the priority should go to the small inshore fleet. However, one must not confuse priority and exclusivity.

October 25, 1979
Adjournment Debate
The hon. member should also recognize the very important benefits of employment which will accrue to those shore based industries which will process this increased quota. I wish to emphasize that consultations were held and that all parties were consulted before the decision was made. It is clear that no amount of additional consultation could have resolved differing views. Therefore it was the minister's responsibility to make the final decision on the basis of those consultations and the best scientific advice available.
It should be noted, Mr. Speaker, that trawlers based outside the Gulf have always fished from this stock.
